hook.text: In most rich countries, five supermarket chains control over 60% of food retail. They set the rules farmers follow.

buildup.text: Supermarkets demand uniform size, perfect appearance, and rock-bottom prices. Food that doesn't comply is rejected.

discovery.text: Up to 40% of farm produce is rejected for cosmetic reasons. Perfectly edible food never leaves the farm.

twist.text: Suppliers absorb price drops while supermarket margins stay stable. The farmer's share of food prices has fallen to 15%.

climax.text: Market concentration gives a handful of buyers enormous power over millions of suppliers worldwide.

punchline.text: The supermarket chooses what you eat—and what the farmer earns.

quiz.question: What share of the retail food price typically goes to the farmer?

details.summary: Supermarket power describes the enormous influence retail chains have over what food gets produced, how it looks, and what farmers earn. This topic covers buyer power, private standards, and how consolidation in retail reshapes the entire food supply chain.
details.whyItMatters: A handful of supermarket chains control the gateway between producers and consumers. Their purchasing decisions determine which farmers survive, what food costs, and how much waste the system generates.
takeaways: In many countries, the top five retailers control over 60% of grocery sales
Supermarket cosmetic standards reject up to 30% of perfectly edible produce
Late payments and last-minute order changes squeeze supplier margins relentlessly

faq.question: How do supermarkets influence the food supply chain?
faq.answer: Supermarkets set cosmetic standards, quality specifications, pricing, and delivery schedules that suppliers must meet. Their concentrated buying power allows them to negotiate aggressively, pushing costs and risks onto farmers and processors.

faq.question: Why does supermarket consolidation concern food system experts?
faq.answer: When a few retailers dominate, farmers have fewer buyers and less bargaining power. This concentration can depress farm-gate prices, reduce product diversity, increase food waste from strict cosmetic standards, and harm rural economies.
